finding.claim: Unauthenticated Marshal.load of attacker-supplied params[:state] in POST /restore allows pre-auth remote code execution via Ruby universal Marshal gadget chains.
finding.source: params[:state] (POST /restore, query string or form body)

trace.note: POST /restore route registered with no authentication or session check
params[:state] is Base64-decoded and passed directly to Marshal.load
state.inspect is returned to the caller, giving an output channel; exploitation does not depend on it

finding.guards_checked: No auth before route; no HMAC/signature on state; Base64 is encoding not a control; no content-type or size check; Ruby Marshal has no safe mode. Only remedy per guides is to stop Marshal-loading untrusted data and use a data-only format such as JSON.

verdict.guard_found: none. app.rb:5 registers POST /restore with no auth, session, or signature check; app.rb:6 passes Base64-decoded params[:state] straight to Marshal.load (Base64 is encoding, not a control); the directory contains only app.rb, so there is no middleware, config.ru, or other auth layer to apply.
verdict.reason: An anonymous HTTP client can POST arbitrary Base64 data to /restore (app.rb:5), which reaches Marshal.load at app.rb:6 with no effective control in between, so this is unauthenticated deserialization of attacker input; the trace matches the code at lines 5–7.

finding.claim: POST /import returns the attacker-controlled top-level JSON object keys unescaped in a text/html response, giving reflected HTML/script injection reachable cross-site via a text/plain form.
finding.source: Top-level keys of JSON request body (request.body.read at app.rb:11)
finding.sink: data.keys.join(",") returned as response body at app.rb:12, Sinatra default Content-Type text/html

trace.note: POST /import route registered with no auth
Raw body parsed with JSON.parse (create_additions off by default, so no object instantiation)
Keys joined and returned unescaped as HTML

finding.guards_checked: JSON.parse without create_additions is safe against object instantiation (not reported). No output encoding. Sinatra default protection set does not cover this (json_csrf applies only to JSON responses). No CSP. Victim must visit attacker page that submits text/plain form whose field name is a JSON fragment, so lower confidence.

verdict.guard_found: Sinatra's default Rack::Protection set, which includes HttpOrigin (app.rb has no `set :protection` override, so it is active). HttpOrigin rejects requests whose Origin header differs from the app's host. A cross-site text/plain form POST from an attacker page carries a cross-origin Origin header, so the browser-driven attack gets a 403 before reaching app.rb:12. No CSP or output encoding is present, and no guard exists inside app.rb itself.
verdict.reason: The trace at app.rb:10-12 is accurate and the route is anonymous, but the cross-site attack the claim depends on is stopped by Sinatra's default HttpOrigin protection (no `set :protection` override in app.rb:1-17), which rejects the cross-origin Origin header a browser sends on a text/plain form POST. This is from my knowledge of Sinatra's default protection list, not from the installed gem, since no Gemfile or lockfile exists in the directory to confirm the version, so the refutation rests on that framework default.
